title: Companies Act, 2013 — Section 54 (Issue of sweat equity shares)

content.overview: Section 54 permits sweat equity shares of a class already issued when its statutory conditions are met, including special-resolution approval and the applicable listed/unlisted regulatory framework.
content.study: Companies Act, 2013 — Section 54. Section 54 permits sweat equity shares of a class already issued when its statutory conditions are met, including special-resolution approval and the applicable listed/unlisted regulatory framework. Apply the statutory ingredients to the facts, check exceptions and connected provisions, and state the legal consequence.

sections.heading: Statutory Rule
sections.body: Section 54 permits sweat equity shares of a class already issued when its statutory conditions are met, including special-resolution approval and the applicable listed/unlisted regulatory framework.

sections.heading: Mandatory Ingredients and Conditions
sections.body: Sweat equity is of a class of shares already issued; Special resolution authorises the issue; Resolution specifies number, current market price, consideration and class/classes of directors or employees; At least one year has elapsed since commencement of business under the statutory condition; Listed company follows applicable SEBI regulations; unlisted company follows prescribed rules

sections.heading: Application and Exceptions
sections.body: Classify the transaction, identify the operative condition or exception, and apply each statutory requirement to the record.

sections.heading: Connected Provisions and Consequences
sections.body: Section 54 is a controlled exception linked to section 53; the Companies (Share Capital and Debentures) Rules and applicable SEBI framework supply additional requirements.

examples.title: Section 54 example 1
examples.body: A company proposes sweat equity to eligible directors/employees; the general meeting passes the required special resolution specifying the prescribed particulars and the company follows applicable rules.

examples.title: Section 54 example 2
examples.body: For a listed company, the issue must also comply with applicable SEBI regulations.

cases.name: Salomon v. A. Salomon & Co. Ltd.
cases.facts: A properly incorporated company was challenged as indistinct from its controlling shareholder.
cases.issue: What is the legal effect of incorporation?
cases.ratioDecidendi: A registered company is a legal person separate from its members, even when control and ownership are concentrated.
cases.holding: The company's separate personality was affirmed.
cases.relevance: Use for Companies Act s. 9 and corporate personality.

cases.name: Foss v. Harbottle
cases.facts: Shareholders sought relief for alleged wrongs to the company.
cases.issue: Who may sue for a wrong done to the company and when may exceptions apply?
cases.ratioDecidendi: The company is the proper plaintiff for corporate wrongs, subject to recognised exceptions such as fraud on the minority and ultra vires acts.
cases.holding: The proper-plaintiff and majority-rule principles were established.
cases.relevance: Use with oppression, mismanagement and class-action analysis.

cases.name: Needle Industries (India) Ltd. v. Needle Industries Newey (India) Holding Ltd.
cases.facts: The Court examined share issue powers and alleged oppression.
cases.issue: When does a corporate action become oppressive or invalid?
cases.ratioDecidendi: The Court examines purpose, fairness, statutory power and resulting prejudice rather than treating every irregularity as oppression.
cases.holding: The corporate action was assessed under the statutory and equitable framework.
cases.relevance: Use for share allotment and oppression claims.

cases.name: Miheer H. Mafatlal v. Mafatlal Industries Ltd.
cases.facts: The Court reviewed a scheme of arrangement sanctioned by the company court.
cases.issue: What is the court's role in sanctioning a corporate scheme?
cases.ratioDecidendi: The court must ensure statutory compliance, class fairness, informed approval and absence of illegality, but does not substitute its commercial judgment for the company's decision.
cases.holding: The principles governing scheme sanction were stated.
cases.relevance: Use for corporate arrangements and tribunal scrutiny.
